title: Guessing coins and dancing in shop doorways for tips
summary: He earns pennies by guessing the coins in grownups' hands and by tapping outside stores, ending with a military-style time step.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Well, then the people used to store money, you know. They had a thing in the South there. I mean this are adults, grownups, they would hold out their hand and say, 'What have I got there?' If the child can guess, you know, say, eenie-meenie-miney-moe (inaudible) in the dough, if he hollers, let him go. I say, 'You got three dimes, two quarters and four nickels,' you know. So they all open up their hand, and that's what they would have. But they would also have eight

pennies, you know, without seeing the pennies. But they open, and I would say "... and" eight pennies. You understand. That's another laugh. So they would give me that, you know. I'd take that. "Thank you, sir. Thank you, ma'am. Sometimes it would be husband and wife, you know. Sometimes they'd be father and daughter, you know, some of those, brother and sister, you see.

But I'd get me -- I'd get me pockets jingling with the money. So then I had another thing with the money. Now I got the little coins, right? So I'd go to another side of the street, you know. I'd get in front of the important store where people coming out, you understand. And I see some people walking or coming out of the place. I make these sounds, like tap dancing, you know, practicing one of the steps, ruh, buh, buh, buh.

I used to take and lift my foot, you know, and tough the display window, you know, and these bottle tops would make this sound, patter, you know, pat, rap, tap. Somebody else would say, "What kind of feet does he got, you know. Did you hear that? Look at that. Who was it? Where did it come from?" You know, see?
So I say "He did it. That? Him? Oh, let's go ask. Let's find out -- or something, you know. And they would say, "Say there, what's your name? And I would say "Boodjie, you know. See?

You understand? So -- but the people -- I could see -- I don't know. I could see happiness in a person's face when it's going to happen, you see, and I would try to exaggerate that. You know, it was an exception, I guess you would call it. You could call it that, conception or exception, either one.
So they would say sometime, 'Can you dance?' Because their idea was to find out where the sound came from.

I'd say -- I'd shake my head up and down -- you know, I'd say some funny way, 'Oh, yeah, oh, yeah, you know. 'Can I?' -- or something, you know, and I'd make a sound. I'd name a song, you know 'Broadway Melody'? That was very popular.

Yeah, and they say, well, 'Who don't?' Or -- 'Do we?' You know, and by the time they say, do we, I'd start to dance. I'd be rattling my foot, you know, tuh-tuh-tuh-tuh-tuh-rappettuh-tuh-tuh-tuh. It was a different time step then, call it -- it was in the military tap. That was the best type of what you call keeping time, you know, being in with the music.
